title: The Puritan Influence: How Spurgeon Became "The Last of the Puritans"

content.text: A Victorian Mind Forged in the Seventeenth Century

Although Charles Haddon Spurgeon lived and ministered entirely within the Victorian era, his theological, intellectual, and spiritual heart was firmly anchored in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. The Puritan movement of that earlier age had profoundly shaped the Protestant landscape of England, producing individuals of immense spiritual stature who combined deep devotional intensity with vigorous intellectual cultivation. Spurgeon drank so deeply from these ancient wells that his contemporaries and later historians rightfully bestowed upon him the distinguished title of "The Last of the Puritans".
The Stambourne Library and Early Immersions

The genesis of this lifelong affinity can be traced back to his early childhood. While living with his grandparents in the rural village of Stambourne, the young boy gained access to a dark, windowless room in the manse that served as a storage space for old books. There, he discovered the massive, dust-covered tomes of the great Puritan divines. Long before he could fully grasp the complex nuances of their theology, Spurgeon was eagerly reading the works of Richard Baxter and John Owen.

However, no author captured his imagination or shaped his soul quite like John Bunyan. Spurgeon found an illustrated copy of The Pilgrim's Progress and was utterly mesmerized by it, eventually reading the masterpiece more than a hundred times over the course of his life. He also devoured John Foxe's Book of Martyrs, adopting the valiant, persecuted Protestants and Puritans of previous centuries as his ultimate heroes.

As Spurgeon matured and his reading deepened, the Puritans became much more than childhood heroes; they became his theological masters and homiletical models. Church historian Mark Hopkins notes that Spurgeon found in the Puritan writings a triumvirate of virtues that was largely missing from the general evangelicalism of his own day: a rigorous theology, a warm spirituality, and a practical applicability.

Spurgeon realized that the Puritans did not separate the life of the mind from the life of the heart. Much like George Whitefield, J. C. Ryle, Martyn Lloyd-Jones, and J. I. Packer, Spurgeon found in the Puritan literature "powerful ammunition to fight the battles of the Lord". He admired them because they held fiercely to the transcendence of God's holiness, the vast gulf of human sinfulness, and the glorious substitutionary atonement that bridged that very gulf. When lecturing to his own pastoral students years later, Spurgeon continually pointed them to the Puritans, urging them to emulate masters like Thomas Brooks, whose works he praised for containing "dust of gold" and an "exceeding preciousness" in holy fancy and metaphor.
A "Bibline" Blood and the Preacher's Library

One of the primary reasons Spurgeon venerated the Puritans was their absolute submission to and saturation with the Holy Scriptures. He viewed them as men whose very constitution had been altered by the Word of God. Speaking of his beloved John Bunyan as the ultimate example of this Puritan ideal, Spurgeon eloquently exhorted: "Read anything of his, and you will see that it is almost like reading the Bible itself. He had studied our Authorized Version... till his whole being was saturated with Scripture... Prick him anywhere; and you will find that his blood is Bibline, the very essence of the Bible flows from him".

To ensure that his own ministry remained tethered to this rich heritage, Spurgeon became a voracious reader and a dedicated collector of books. He amassed an enormous personal library that eventually reached 12,000 volumes. Astoundingly, this collection included around one thousand rare works published before the year 1700—the golden age of Puritanism. From this massive theological arsenal, he drew the deep, Reformed, and experiential truths that would feed his congregation of thousands at the Metropolitan Tabernacle.
The Enduring Legacy of "The Last Puritan"

Spurgeon's unyielding commitment to the Puritan theology of grace provided the bedrock for his resistance against the creeping liberalism of his time. While the spirit of the age embraced higher criticism and pragmatism, Spurgeon stood firm as an heir of the reformers. He did not view his Calvinism as a novel invention but recognized that the ancient truths he preached were the exact same truths championed by Augustine, John Calvin, and the faithful Puritans before him. By intertwining a robust, sovereign-grace theology with a burning passion for the lost, Charles Spurgeon successfully brought the spiritual vitality of the seventeenth-century Puritans into the heart of the modern industrial world.
